children: U.S. nonresidential construction starts continued to expand in August, with a massive increase in data-center projects helping offset weakness in infrastructure, according to a UBS analysis of Dodge Data & Analytics figures.

Total nonresidential construction starts rose 5.8% from a year earlier in August, while starts over the latest three months increased 17.4%. On a six-month basis, starts were up 25.8%, and the trailing 12-month increase was 22.1%, UBS analyst Steven Fisher and his team said in a Sept. 22 report.
Data centers lead building boom

The headline August figure masks a sharp divergence between building construction and infrastructure. Building starts jumped 31.8% from a year earlier, led by a 248% increase in data centers. Manufacturing starts rose 33%, government buildings surged 201% and hotel construction increased 55%.
The data-center expansion looks even more striking over longer periods. Starts in the category increased 262% on a three-month basis, 246% over six months and 197% over the trailing 12 months.

For investors, the figures provide further evidence that spending tied to artificial intelligence and cloud computing is becoming an increasingly important driver of U.S. construction activity. UBS expects nonresidential construction spending to reaccelerate in the second half of 2026, supported by data centers, power projects, manufacturing including semiconductor and pharmaceutical facilities, and infrastructure. Construction starts are an important leading indicator because projects can take years to complete, translating today's starts into future spending on equipment, engineering, materials and labor.

UBS now forecasts nominal U.S. nonresidential construction spending will increase 6.7% in 2027 after declining 0.9% in 2026. Its previous forecast called for 6% growth next year following 3% growth this year.
Infrastructure hits speed bump

Infrastructure provided a counterweight to the building boom. Monthly infrastructure starts fell 21.5% from a year earlier after increasing 9.2% in July. Streets and highways declined 27.6%, bridges fell 38% and power plant and gas-related starts dropped 19.3%. Dams, reservoirs and river-development projects were a notable exception, rising 69%.

The longer-term picture remains considerably stronger. Infrastructure starts were up 23.1% over the latest six months and 27.6% over 12 months. Power starts increased 54% and 88%, respectively, over those periods.

UBS said the recent infrastructure weakness may be related to uncertainty surrounding the expiration of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act at the end of September and its extension through December. The firm said that could leave the sector subdued until there is greater clarity about longer-term federal funding.
Traditional commercial construction weak

Not all building markets are participating in the expansion. Warehouse starts fell 21.7% in August and were down 17.7% over the trailing 12 months. Office construction excluding data centers declined 15% in August, highlighting how much data-center investment is distorting the broader office category.
UBS expects commercial construction to recover slowly because of elevated long-term interest rates and projects spending in the category will remain negative through the end of 2026.
The investment implications extend across a broad group of industrial and materials companies. UBS identified machinery companies including Caterpillar
, Deere
and United Rentals
; engineering and construction companies including Quanta Services
, Jacobs Solutions
, Fluor
and EMCOR
; and steel and materials producers including Nucor
, Steel Dynamics
, Martin Marietta Materials
and Vulcan Materials
as having exposure to U.S. nonresidential construction.
